ocar.opportunity: Synapse-level connectomes show that developing neurons contact many cell types yet synapse with only a subset. Pairing those maps with cell-type transcriptomes and cell-adhesion-molecule binding tables could identify receptor–ligand pairs that match synaptic partners.
ocar.challenge: Many CAM families contribute to wiring, but it has been hard to name receptor–ligand pairs that directly match neurons to their synaptic targets amid circuit complexity.
ocar.action: Yoo, Dombrovski, Zipursky, Kurmangaliyev and colleagues, in Current Biology (2023), integrate a Drosophila visual-system synapse-level connectome with developmental CAM expression and binding specificities, focusing on genetically related T4/T5 subtypes that choose alternative targets in adjacent neuropil layers.
ocar.resolution: Layer choice correlates with matching Beat and Side family receptor–ligand pairs on synaptic partners. Genetic analysis shows that presynaptic Side-II and postsynaptic Beat-VI restrict partners to the same layer; removing the pair disrupts layers and causes inappropriate targeting of presynaptic sites and postsynaptic dendrites.
ocar.future_work: The authors propose that different Side/Beat pairs collaborate with other recognition molecules, and that combining transcriptomes, connectomes, and protein interactomes can identify wiring determinants more generally.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly visual neurons pick specific partners among many nearby cells. This paper matches wiring maps with gene and protein-binding data and finds adhesive receptor–ligand pairs that keep related motion-sensing cells in the correct layers.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Biology (2023), Yoo and colleagues integrate a Drosophila visual connectome with developmental cell-adhesion-molecule expression and binding specificities. Closely related T4/T5 motion-detection subtypes choose alternative targets in adjacent layers, correlating with distinct Beat/Side receptor–ligand pairs. Presynaptic Side-II and postsynaptic Beat-VI restrict partners to the same layer; loss of the pair disrupts layers and mistargets pre- and postsynaptic processes.
summaries.advanced: The attached PDF extract is a different paper (Krishnan et al. on C. elegans interciliary contacts); this annotation follows the catalog abstract only and does not use numbers from that extract. The Side-II/Beat-VI genetic result is specific to T4/T5 layer choice, not a complete wiring code. Collaboration with other recognition molecules is proposed, not fully mapped. Catalog organism is fly.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly visual neurons pick specific partners among many nearby cells. This paper matches wiring maps with gene and protein-binding data and finds adhesive receptor–ligand pairs that keep related motion-sensing cells in the correct layers.

ocar.opportunity: Neurons underpin animal cognition, but the evolutionary and mechanistic roots of even elementary cognition remain unclear. Independent origins of neural and neuroid systems, plus a chemical connectome of volume transmission, offer comparative experiments that synaptic wiring diagrams alone do not.
ocar.challenge: How neurons originated, and how ensembles generate stereotyped and learned behavior, is unknown. Dynamic chemical micro-environments and cell-specific volume transmission are poorly measured, so links from chemistry to behavior are missing.
ocar.action: Moroz and Romanova, in Animal Cognition (2023), review evidence that neural and other integrative systems evolved more than once among basal metazoans, and they introduce chemoconnectomics as the study of hundreds of signal molecules operating in tandem with classical synapses.
ocar.resolution: They highlight ctenophore nervous systems and neuroid-like systems in placozoans and sponges as independent experiments. They argue that roughly 20 classical transmitters plus 100+ peptides and hundreds of receptors expand information capacity, with nitric oxide as a shared non-synaptic integrator across basal metazoans and choanoflagellates, and that ctenophores use a largely different transmitter set than cnidarians and bilaterians.
ocar.future_work: They call for new tools linking orchestrated volume transmission to behavior, and for studying early-branching lineages as alternative integrative systems to decipher chemical syntaxes of cognition.

summaries.beginner: Animal thinking is often treated as a product of wired nerve cells, but much signaling is chemical and may have evolved more than once. This review argues we should map those chemical conversations, especially in comb jellies, placozoans, and sponges.
summaries.intermediate: In Animal Cognition (2023), Moroz and Romanova argue that integrative systems evolved convergently among basal metazoans and that a chemical connectome of volume transmission is the most information-rich source of adaptability. They cite ctenophore neurons versus neuroid systems in placozoans and sponges, and they tally molecular diversity on the order of ~20 classical transmitters, 100+ peptides, and usually several hundred receptors. They frame chemoconnectomics plus cellular behavior in early-branching lineages as a foundation for studying elementary cognition.
summaries.advanced: This is a conceptual review, not a new connectome. Counts of transmitters and peptides are order-of-magnitude statements in the conclusion, not a census of one species. Cognition is used broadly (including non-neural examples such as bacteria and Physarum). Catalog stage is infrastructure; there is no EM reconstruction here.

plain_language_summary: Animal thinking is often treated as a product of wired nerve cells, but much signaling is chemical and may have evolved more than once. This review argues we should map those chemical conversations, especially in comb jellies, placozoans, and sponges.

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section multibeam SEM can collect cubic-millimeter-scale neural volumes at synaptic resolution, creating petabyte datasets that can become connectomes. Those volumes exist only after hundreds of millions of image tiles are aligned into a 3D stack.
ocar.challenge: A cubic-millimeter mSEM dataset comprises hundreds of millions of tiles (each 15.5 × 13.5 μm² in the authors’ Zeiss multiSEM setup). Alignment must keep navigation smooth in all directions while minimizing section distortions relative to the original micrographs, including missing sections and thickness variation.
ocar.action: Watkins, Jelli, and Briggman introduce msemalign in Frontiers in Neuroscience (2023): a scalable, relatively simple pipeline for ssmSEM volume alignment, used with customized sectioning and parallel multiSEM acquisition aimed at petabyte-scale datasets.
ocar.resolution: They report that the pipeline can align petabyte-scale data with smooth transitions while limiting overall section distortion versus the acquired micrographs. Contrast correction uses histogram matching to a template rather than CLAHE-style equalization, to avoid flattening real tissue differences such as soma versus neuropil.
ocar.future_work: They suggest richer multi-algorithm keypoint matching for missing sections and multiple template histograms for long z-stacks as practical enhancements.

summaries.beginner: Giant electron-microscope brain volumes are photographed as millions of tiny overlapping tiles that must be stitched into a smooth 3D picture. This paper describes software built to do that stitching at huge scale without warping the original photos more than necessary.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroscience (2023), Watkins, Jelli, and Briggman present msemalign for serial-section multibeam SEM alignment. They target ~1 mm³ or larger synaptic-resolution volumes whose acquisition yields hundreds of millions of tiles. Design goals are scalability, simple architecture, smooth 3D navigation, and minimal distortion relative to original micrographs, with template histogram matching to preserve tissue appearance.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods paper; the selected text does not report a completed connectome or numeric alignment-error tables. Tile size 15.5 × 13.5 μm² is specific to their multiSEM configuration. Catalog tags include mouse and DS13 MICrONS, but the paper is a general ssmSEM alignment pipeline rather than a MICrONS data release. Distortion minimization is qualitative in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Giant electron-microscope brain volumes are photographed as millions of tiny overlapping tiles that must be stitched into a smooth 3D picture. This paper describes software built to do that stitching at huge scale without warping the original photos more than necessary.

ocar.opportunity: EM connectomes have clarified fly visual computations, but the lobula—thought to detect object-like features and drive behaviors via LC and LPLC outputs—still lacked a map of columnar inputs onto those outputs.
ocar.challenge: Available dense reconstructions often omit upstream visual neuropils that would normally identify lobula inputs, leaving fragmented axon terminals that are hard to type.
ocar.action: Tanaka and Clark, in eNeuro (2022), cluster fragmented lobula terminals in the hemibrain connectome by connectivity and morphology, then match clusters to previously described cell types.
ocar.resolution: They extract 40 clusters with homogeneous connectivity and morphology and morphologically match 24, with highest confidence for T3 (clusters 1–4), T2 (5), TmY29 and/or Tm28 (10), Tm20 (17), Tm9 (30), and TmY11 (35). Other assignments (including TmY5a as cluster 40) are more speculative. They report previously undocumented input–output connectivity usable as hypotheses for feature detection.
ocar.future_work: They state that more complete reconstructions are required to verify the map, and they point to molecular tracing (GRASP, trans-Tango, optogenetics) as complementary tests.

summaries.beginner: A part of the fruit-fly visual brain is thought to spot objects such as other flies, but many of its incoming wires were unnamed fragments. This study groups those fragments by shape and connections and proposes which known cell types they are.
summaries.intermediate: In eNeuro (2022), Tanaka and Clark cluster columnar inputs to Drosophila lobula in the hemibrain EM volume despite missing upstream neuropils. Among 40 clusters, 24 receive morphological matches of varying confidence, with strongest IDs for T3, T2, TmY29/Tm28, Tm20, Tm9, and TmY11. They report previously undocumented synapses onto lobula output neurons (LC/LPLC and related types) as a basis for physiological hypotheses.
summaries.advanced: The hemibrain largely lacks medulla and lobula plate, so input identities are inferred from terminal morphology and local connectivity, not from complete cells. Many type assignments are explicitly speculative. Per-cell synapse counts onto named outputs (e.g., cluster 40 onto LC10 at 4.3 synapses/cell) are cluster means, not circuit proofs. Catalog has no named dataset tag; the volume is hemibrain.

plain_language_summary: A part of the fruit-fly visual brain is thought to spot objects such as other flies, but many of its incoming wires were unnamed fragments. This study groups those fragments by shape and connections and proposes which known cell types they are.

ocar.opportunity: Drosophila melanogaster offers a near-term path to understanding a whole brain: roughly 200,000 neurons, rich behavior, and many experimental tools. An EM-level list of neurons and chemical synapses is expected within a few years.
ocar.challenge: A wiring diagram alone will not explain how the brain operates. The field still needs to specify what additional data must be collected and organized to build an integrated model.
ocar.action: Scheffer and Meinertzhagen, in Journal of Experimental Biology (2021), itemize the measurements they argue are still required—beyond the coming connectome—to understand structure and operation of the fly brain.
ocar.resolution: The essay is a requirements list for an integrated model rather than a new dataset: it treats the connectome as necessary but not sufficient and enumerates missing physiological, molecular, and behavioral ingredients.
ocar.future_work: Collating and organizing those additional data types is presented as the work still needed once the connectome exists.

summaries.beginner: A complete wiring diagram of a fruit-fly brain is nearly in hand, but wires alone do not explain behavior. This essay asks what else—activity, chemistry, and experiments—still has to be measured to understand that brain.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Experimental Biology (2021), Scheffer and Meinertzhagen argue that Drosophila, with on the order of 200,000 neurons, is an enticing whole-brain target. They take an imminent EM connectome of neurons and chemical synapses as given and catalog further data needed for an integrated model of how the brain works.
summaries.advanced: The attached PDF extract is a different paper (Pugliese et al. on a walking CPG); this annotation follows the catalog abstract only. This is a perspective, not new reconstructions. The ~200,000-neuron figure is the authors’ order of magnitude. Chemical synapses are the stated connectome contents; electrical synapses and neuromodulation are among the implied gaps.

plain_language_summary: A complete wiring diagram of a fruit-fly brain is nearly in hand, but wires alone do not explain behavior. This essay asks what else—activity, chemistry, and experiments—still has to be measured to understand that brain.

ocar.opportunity: Complete C. elegans connectomes now exist at multiple ages, so graph and motif tools can summarize how a whole wiring diagram changes through development instead of inspecting every neuron by hand.
ocar.challenge: Synapse-resolution datasets are already too large to proofread neuron by neuron. The task is to find which network patterns are stable, which grow, and which decay unexpectedly across time points.
ocar.action: Matelsky, Gray-Roncal and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2021), apply graph-analysis and motif-atlas scans (via DotMotif) to C. elegans connectomes at multiple developmental stages, comparing undirected subgraphs of six or fewer neurons.
ocar.resolution: They report changing local structure: the most rapidly growing undirected motif is 353 times more frequent in Dataset 8 than in Dataset 1, whereas triangles and the triangular-prism net grow only about 9.24× and 9.33×. They present these stable and shifting invariants as a substrate for further analysis.
ocar.future_work: Software (dotmotif, grand) is shared; they frame the nematode as a preview of comparative graph analysis in flies, mice, and humans.

summaries.beginner: As a worm grows, its wiring diagram changes in patterned ways. This preprint counts small repeating circuit shapes across ages and shows that some shapes explode in number while others barely keep pace.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2021), Matelsky et al. compare C. elegans connectomes across developmental time points with graph metrics and an undirected motif atlas. Relative to the earliest dataset, one six-or-fewer-neuron motif increases 353-fold by Dataset 8, while triangles and a triangular-prism motif increase only ~9-fold. Tools are released at github.com/aplbrain/dotmotif and grand.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint. Motif fold-changes are ratios to Dataset 1, not absolute synapse counts, and depend on the Witvliet-style multi-age reconstructions cited as (4,5). Analyses are undirected in the highlighted atlas scan. Catalog dataset is DS01 C. elegans (White+).

plain_language_summary: As a worm grows, its wiring diagram changes in patterned ways. This preprint counts small repeating circuit shapes across ages and shows that some shapes explode in number while others barely keep pace.

ocar.opportunity: High-throughput 3D electron microscopy now lets the same cortical volume type be mapped at many postnatal ages, so inhibitory circuit formation can be quantified synapse by synapse rather than inferred from single snapshots.
ocar.challenge: A comprehensive map of how cortical inhibitory axons acquire preferences for cell bodies, apical dendrites, and axon initial segments during postnatal development was missing.
ocar.action: Gour, Helmstaedter and colleagues, in Science (2020), analyze 13 three-dimensional EM datasets from mouse somatosensory cortex layers 4 and 2/3 at postnatal days 5, 7, 9, 14, 28, and 56, reconstructing inhibitory innervation of those compartments.
ocar.resolution: Apical-dendrite preference is already near adult levels at P5. Soma-targeting axons acquire specificity mainly between P7 and P9, with cell-body preference increasing almost threefold and synapse density along those axons dropping almost twofold, consistent with removal of off-target synapses. Chandelier axo-axonic preference is first clear by P14 and nearly complete by P28, reaching about 50% of axon-initial-segment synaptic input, with cartridges forming after preference begins.
ocar.future_work: They present connectomic screening across ages as a template for later genetic or environmental perturbations of circuit formation.

summaries.beginner: Inhibitory brain cells must learn which parts of other cells to contact as a mouse grows. Electron-microscope maps at many ages show that some targeting is present from the start, while other targeting is sculpted by removing misplaced contacts.
summaries.intermediate: In Science (2020), Gour et al. map inhibitory synaptogenesis in mouse somatosensory cortex with 13 3D EM volumes spanning P5–P56 (focus on the first four postnatal weeks). Apical-dendrite preference is early; soma preference rises sharply from P5 to P9 with synaptic overabundance then removal; chandelier AIS preference develops from P14 to P28. The work is framed as developmental connectomic screening of barrel-related cortex.
summaries.advanced: The attached PDF extract is a different paper (Zhang et al. 2026 ssEM inpainting); this annotation follows the catalog abstract only. Time points include P56 as adult comparison. “Almost threefold” and “almost twofold” are abstract phrasing, not exact ratios. Dataset tag DS12 L4 barrel cortex matches the somatosensory focus; L2/3 is also imaged.

plain_language_summary: Inhibitory brain cells must learn which parts of other cells to contact as a mouse grows. Electron-microscope maps at many ages show that some targeting is present from the start, while other targeting is sculpted by removing misplaced contacts.

ocar.opportunity: Mesoscale connectomics maps connections among neuronal populations, filling the gap between single-synapse ultrastructure and whole-region anatomy. Decades of tract tracing now sit beside viral, genetic, and imaging tools that can target defined cell classes.
ocar.challenge: Newcomers face an intersectional toolbox spanning molecular biology, virology, microscopy, computer science, and genetics. Analysis and sharing of tracing data remain bottlenecks.
ocar.action: Saleeba, Dempsey, Goodchild, McMullan and colleagues review, in Frontiers in Neuroscience (2019), mesoscale methods from a student’s perspective: history, conventional and viral anterograde and retrograde tracers, and strategies for selecting neuronal subpopulations, plus weaknesses in analysis and dissemination.
ocar.resolution: The review inventories reagents that can identify efferent and afferent connectomes of selected populations and flags current bottlenecks. The authors conclude that connectomic data will not by itself explain how brains work, because connectivity is only one classification axis.
ocar.future_work: They discuss likely trajectories of rapidly developing neuroanatomy technologies and remaining needs for analysis and data sharing.

summaries.beginner: There are now many ways to label who talks to whom in the mammalian brain, from old dyes to engineered viruses. This student-oriented review explains those tools and warns that a wiring list is only one of several ways to classify neurons.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroscience (2019), Saleeba et al. survey mesoscale tract tracing for novices, covering conventional and viral tracers and genetic selection of subpopulations. They assess analysis and dissemination bottlenecks and emphasize that connectivity is one parameter among overlapping neuronal classifications, not a complete explanation of function.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods review of light-level tracing, not EM connectomics, despite the catalog proofreading tag. No new quantitative circuit is reported. Catalog organism and dataset fields are empty.

plain_language_summary: There are now many ways to label who talks to whom in the mammalian brain, from old dyes to engineered viruses. This student-oriented review explains those tools and warns that a wiring list is only one of several ways to classify neurons.

ocar.opportunity: Fly motion detection is a classic test of circuit models, and ON-pathway (T4) connectomes already showed that real wiring is more intricate than a two-input Hassenstein–Reichardt detector. A matching OFF-pathway (T5) map in the same volume would let the two edges be compared directly.
ocar.challenge: T5 input anatomy was incomplete. Reconstructing inputs to both T4 and T5 across an entire optic lobe requires automated synapse prediction at connectome scale.
ocar.action: Shinomiya, Meinertzhagen, Plaza and colleagues, in eLife (2019), reconstruct a single EM optic-lobe volume covering inputs to both T4 and T5, using automated synapse prediction suited to a large connectome.
ocar.resolution: They corroborate prior T4 findings and comprehensively identify T5 inputs and receptive-field composition. They map a three-legged scheme onto anatomy: for T4, Mi1/Tm3 as direct inputs, Mi9 as enhancer, and CT1/Mi4/C3 as suppressors; for T5, Tm1/Tm2/Tm4 as direct, Tm9 as enhancer, and CT1 as the only inhibitory columnar input, displaced from the excitatory legs. Similarities and differences are proposed to underlie distinct ON versus OFF properties.
ocar.future_work: They note that silencing data (e.g., a large Tm9 contribution to dark-edge detection) may not map one-to-one onto anatomical enhancer/suppressor labels, so physiology remains needed to weight the legs.

summaries.beginner: Fruit flies sense moving light and dark edges with two related circuits. This paper maps both in one electron-microscope volume and shows they share a three-input layout but are not wired identically.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2019), Shinomiya et al. present an optic-lobe EM connectome integrating T4 (ON) and T5 (OFF) motion pathways. Automated synapse prediction supports corroboration of T4 inputs and a comprehensive T5 input list. They interpret the maps with a three-input elementary-motion-detector model (direct, delayed enhancer, delayed suppressor) and highlight CT1 as T5’s sole inhibitory columnar input.
summaries.advanced: “Conclusive and comprehensive” refers to columnar inputs in this optic-lobe volume, not a whole-brain connectome. Enhancer/suppressor labels are model assignments onto anatomy, and the authors themselves flag mismatches with silencing of Tm9. Evolutionary linkage of T4 and T5 is stated as probable. Catalog stage is synapses; organism is fly.

plain_language_summary: Fruit flies sense moving light and dark edges with two related circuits. This paper maps both in one electron-microscope volume and shows they share a three-input layout but are not wired identically.

ocar.opportunity: Reconstructing neurons from 3D electron microscopy is a core connectomics bottleneck. Dense voxel embeddings from deep metric learning could replace boundary detection with an object-centered representation that is also reusable for later agglomeration.
ocar.challenge: Boundary-detection nets still led SNEMI3D and CREMI leaderboards; flood-filling and related object-centric methods had not displaced them. Thin processes and self-contact motifs systematically cause splits.
ocar.action: Lee, Lu, Luther, and Seung, in IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging (catalog year 2019; arXiv 2021 revision), train a convolutional net to embed voxels so same-object pairs are close, build a metric graph, partition it with long-range repulsive edges (Mutex Watershed), then reuse the same net to agglomerate self-contact splits.
ocar.resolution: They report state-of-the-art 3D neuron reconstruction on serial-section EM, with substantial accuracy gain on very thin objects, including glia. A SNEMI3D figure caption lists an adapted Rand error of 0.0249 with test-time augmentation versus 0.0314 for a 2017 mean-affinity agglomeration submission.
ocar.future_work: They suggest the embedding representation may serve other automated circuit-reconstruction tasks beyond this segmentation recipe.

summaries.beginner: Computers must color in every nerve cell in a 3D brain picture without breaking thin branches. This method teaches a network to give nearby bits of the same cell similar codes, then groups them, and is especially helpful for very skinny processes.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging (2019 catalog year), Lee et al. segment serial-section EM with dense voxel embeddings, a metric graph, Mutex Watershed using long-range repulsion, and mean-embedding agglomeration for self-contact. They claim SOTA versus a leading boundary-detection baseline on SNEMI3D-style reconstruction, with remaining splits where conservative repulsion and agglomeration heuristics fail on complex glia self-contacts.
summaries.advanced: Leaderboard adapted Rand numbers (0.0249 vs 0.0314) come from a supplementary figure caption and should not be treated as a full ablation table. Catalog year is 2019 while the DOI is a 2021 TMI article. Organism is unspecified; method tag is serial-section EM. Self-contact remains a residual failure mode.

plain_language_summary: Computers must color in every nerve cell in a 3D brain picture without breaking thin branches. This method teaches a network to give nearby bits of the same cell similar codes, then groups them, and is especially helpful for very skinny processes.

ocar.opportunity: Automated neuron reconstruction from volume EM usually needs dataset-specific volumetric labels that are slow to paint. If images from a new microscope or stain could be translated into the appearance of a dataset that already has labels, a trained segmenter could be reused.
ocar.challenge: Ordinary augmentation does not capture inter-dataset appearance shifts. One cited prior study spent 408 hours annotating 131 million voxels of songbird brain for a single training set. Domain translation must preserve membranes if transferred flood-filling is to be valid.
ocar.action: Januszewski and Jain, on bioRxiv (2019), train Segmentation-Enhanced CycleGAN (SECGAN): unsupervised image-to-image translation regularized by a flood-filling network, then apply an FFN trained on SNEMI ground truth to SegEM images after translation.
ocar.resolution: They report near-perfect reconstruction accuracy on a benchmark connectomics segmentation dataset in a zero-shot setting where the segmenter never saw volumetric labels from the target imaging method. They argue SECGAN reduces or eliminates new ground-truth annotation.
ocar.future_work: They caution that local ultrastructure tasks such as synapse detection need separate evaluation, even if neuron-scale reconstruction appears unbiased.

summaries.beginner: Each new electron-microscope brain volume usually needs a custom training set painted by people. This preprint translates pictures from one volume into the style of another so an existing tracing program can be reused without new labels.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2019), Januszewski and Jain introduce SECGAN, adding segmentation-derived losses to CycleGAN so volume-EM images can be translated between domains. An FFN trained on SNEMI labels is applied to SegEM after SegEM→SNEMI translation, which they contrast with a CLAHE-only baseline. They describe near-perfect zero-shot reconstruction on a benchmark and position the method as reducing annotation burden.
summaries.advanced: “Near perfect” is qualitative in the abstract; the selected text does not quote a numeric error rate for the zero-shot test. The 408-hour / 131-million-voxel figure is from a prior songbird study, not this paper’s labeling cost. Synapse detection after translation is explicitly not validated. This is a preprint.

plain_language_summary: Each new electron-microscope brain volume usually needs a custom training set painted by people. This preprint translates pictures from one volume into the style of another so an existing tracing program can be reused without new labels.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomes describe anatomy but not the molecules that implement physiology. Cell-type transcriptomes aligned to those maps could identify transmitters, receptors, and shared programs across a circuit.
ocar.challenge: Most genomic surveys sample diversity rather than genetically identified circuit cells. Driver lines can include off-target cells, and sparse types yield few nuclei.
ocar.action: Davis, Nern, Rubin, Eddy, Henry and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2018/2019 version), combine Drosophila split-GAL4 drivers, TAPIN-seq nuclear RNA, and a probabilistic interpreter to profile 100 driver lines covering 67 cell types (resource at opticlobe.com), including 53 visual-system types.
ocar.resolution: They report transmitter assignments including co-release, receptor-based functional hypotheses, and commonalities among types, and they integrate the catalogs with optic-lobe connectomes from synapses to pathways. TAPIN’s two-step capture is described as more specific and higher-throughput than one-step INTACT; most neurons express genes for a single transmitter type.
ocar.future_work: They note that some drivers label extra types, that photoreceptors and T4 yielded few nuclei under an earlier protocol, and that sparser lines can still fail quality filters—motivating still-cleaner intersections.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram does not say which chemical each cell uses. This resource measures gene activity in dozens of genetically labeled fruit-fly visual cells and posts the catalog for use with existing connection maps.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2018), Davis et al. release TAPIN-seq transcriptomes for 100 Drosophila driver lines covering 67 cell types (53 in the visual system), at http://www.opticlobe.com. They combine genetic access, tandem affinity purification of nuclei, and probabilistic interpretation, then overlay transmitters and receptors on optic-lobe connectomes, including motion-circuit cells.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint resource paper. Off-target driver labeling is acknowledged as usually minor. Nucleus yield failed for some sparse types under INTACT-like protocols. Catalog stage is segmentation, which does not match the genomic methods. Integration with connectomes is interpretive, not a new EM volume.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram does not say which chemical each cell uses. This resource measures gene activity in dozens of genetically labeled fruit-fly visual cells and posts the catalog for use with existing connection maps.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomes and synaptic-plasticity studies need locations and shapes of chemical synapses, including 30–60 nm clefts that light microscopy cannot resolve. Fully automated 3D reconstruction would reduce manual validation.
ocar.challenge: Existing detectors were not accurate enough to recover connectivity reliably or to cut validation burden, especially across both anisotropic and isotropic EM.
ocar.action: Xiao, Han and colleagues, in BMC Bioinformatics (2018), detect synapses with Faster R-CNN, suppress false positives using z-continuity, and segment clefts with Dijkstra plus GrabCut, validating against manual tracking on anisotropic and isotropic volumes.
ocar.resolution: They report average detection precision of 92.8% (anisotropic) and 93.5% (isotropic) and segmentation precision of 88.6% and 93.0%, respectively, claiming state-of-the-art fully automated 3D synapse reconstruction.
ocar.future_work: They still describe cleft segmentation as somewhat tedious relative to detection and present the pipeline as a rapid source of synaptic statistics for neurologists.

summaries.beginner: Finding every tiny contact in electron-microscope pictures is slow by hand. This software spots synapses, throws out likely false alarms using neighboring slices, and outlines the gap between cells, with high reported precision.
summaries.intermediate: In BMC Bioinformatics (2018), Xiao et al. combine Faster R-CNN detection, z-continuity filtering, and Dijkstra–GrabCut cleft segmentation on EM. Manual validation supports average detection precision of 92.8%/93.5% and segmentation precision of 88.6%/93.0% on anisotropic versus isotropic volumes. They target chemical synapses whose clefts are 30–60 nm.
summaries.advanced: Precision figures are averages on the authors’ test volumes, not a public challenge leaderboard. Partner identity (which two neurons) is not solved by cleft segmentation alone. Organism and dataset are unspecified. “State-of-the-art” is the authors’ claim against methods they compare in the paper.

plain_language_summary: Finding every tiny contact in electron-microscope pictures is slow by hand. This software spots synapses, throws out likely false alarms using neighboring slices, and outlines the gap between cells, with high reported precision.

ocar.opportunity: Hub neurons that form a rich club are a conserved network motif. Mouse and human studies linked hubs to coupled expression of metabolic genes; asking whether C. elegans hubs share a transcriptional signature tests conservation down to identified neurons.
ocar.challenge: Coupled expression could be a trivial consequence of cell class, distance, transmitter, birth time, lineage, or module rather than hub identity per se.
ocar.action: Arnatkevičiūtė, Fulcher, Pocock, and Fornito, in PLOS Computational Biology (2018), combine chemical and electrical connectivity of 279 C. elegans neurons with binary expression of 948 genes, scoring correlated expression for every pair.
ocar.resolution: Hub–hub connections are the most transcriptionally similar and nonhub–nonhub the least. Contributing genes implicate glutamatergic and cholinergic signaling. The coupling is not explained by sensory/motor/interneuron class, distance, transmitter, birth time, lineage distance, or module, but is tied to most hubs being command interneurons that regulate locomotion.
ocar.future_work: They suggest a conserved genomic signature of hubs related to higher-order behavior, inviting tests in other species and scales.

summaries.beginner: Some worm neurons are unusually well connected, like busy hubs. Those hubs also tend to turn on similar genes, not because they sit near each other, but because many of them are the command cells that help the animal crawl.
summaries.intermediate: In PLOS Computational Biology (2018), Arnatkevičiūtė et al. relate the 279-neuron C. elegans connectome to binary expression of 948 genes. Rich-club hub pairs show the highest expression similarity, driven by communication-related genes, and the effect tracks command-interneuron identity rather than proximity or lineage. Data are from public sources with a figshare package.
summaries.advanced: Expression data are binary, not quantitative RNA-seq. The connectome is the canonical 279-neuron chemical-plus-electrical graph, not a new EM volume. Conservation with mouse oxidative-metabolism signatures is analogical: worm genes highlighted here are signaling genes. Catalog dataset is DS01 C. elegans (White+).

plain_language_summary: Some worm neurons are unusually well connected, like busy hubs. Those hubs also tend to turn on similar genes, not because they sit near each other, but because many of them are the command cells that help the animal crawl.

ocar.opportunity: NeuromedinU regulates feeding and activity in mammals; Drosophila hugin neurons have analogous effects. A complete EM connectome of hugin cells could show how a conserved peptide system is wired, including fast synaptic transmission beside neuromodulation.
ocar.challenge: Peptidergic anatomy was known in outline, but synaptic partners, transmitters, and links from chemosensory input to endocrine output were fragmentary.
ocar.action: Schlegel, Cardona, Pankratz and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2016), reconstruct the entire connectome of hugin-producing neurons in the Drosophila larval CNS, test transmitters, and compare peptide-receptor versus synaptic routes.
ocar.resolution: Hugin neurons use acetylcholine as a key co-transmitter; both peptide and acetylcholine are necessary for feeding regulation. Subtypes connect chemosensory pathways to endocrine cells producing DH44 (CRH-like) and insulin-like peptides—homologs also downstream of neuromedinU. Four projection classes have distinct partners rather than one coordinated “hugin phenotype.”
ocar.future_work: They propose a conserved physiological control system at functional, molecular, and network-architecture levels, and they note morphology and feeding-brake roles appear similar from larva to adult, inviting adult connectomic comparison.

summaries.beginner: A small set of fly neurons uses a peptide related to a mammalian hunger signal. Mapping every contact of those cells shows they also use a fast chemical transmitter and sit between taste sensors and hormone cells.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2016), Schlegel et al. reconstruct all hugin neurons in the Drosophila larval EM volume. They report cholinergic synaptic transmission in parallel with hugin peptide, necessity of both for feeding control, and class-specific synaptic plus peptide-receptor links onto DH44 and insulinergic endocrine neurons, arguing homology with neuromedinU pathways.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint. “Entire connectome” is of hugin cells in the larval CNS, not the whole larva. Functional necessity claims are from the paper’s experiments as stated in the abstract; detailed n are not in the selected extract. Catalog dataset is DS03 Drosophila larva.

plain_language_summary: A small set of fly neurons uses a peptide related to a mammalian hunger signal. Mapping every contact of those cells shows they also use a fast chemical transmitter and sit between taste sensors and hormone cells.

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section EM samples depth by cutting or milling, so axial spacing is uneven, sections can be out of order, and FIB-SEM can show wavy non-planar distortion. Image-based correction would recover geometry without extra hardware.
ocar.challenge: Ultramicrotome thickness varies within and between sections (nominal ssTEM often 30–90 nm); manual collection frequently misorders sections; shearing, folds, and stains break simple similarity. FIB-SEM has a distinctive “wave” axial distortion.
ocar.action: Hanslovsky, Bogovic, and Saalfeld (Bioinformatics; arXiv 2016 revision) estimate and correct continuous and discontinuous non-planar axial distortion from image similarity alone, and they sort unordered series, implemented in Fiji and Spark.
ocar.resolution: Proof-of-principle and real-world tests are reported to perform well, including large datasets. They argue combined alignment and series sorting can cut manual intervention in ssTEM, and that non-planar correction addresses the FIB-SEM wave problem.
ocar.future_work: They note that noise limits fine fields of view and that domain-specific models could outperform their mild monotonic-similarity assumptions.

summaries.beginner: When brain tissue is sliced for the electron microscope, slices are not perfectly even or always in order, which warps the 3D picture. This paper infers the true spacing and order from the images themselves and offers free software to correct it.
summaries.intermediate: In Bioinformatics (2015; arXiv 2016), Hanslovsky, Bogovic, and Saalfeld correct axial distortion in serial-section microscopy without extra measurements, targeting ssTEM and FIB-SEM connectomics. Methods use pairwise similarity (monotonic decrease, locally constant similarity-curve shape) to estimate thickness/order and non-planar warp. Code is in Fiji and for HPC (section-sort, z-spacing, z-spacing-spark).
summaries.advanced: Quantitative error tables are not in the selected extract; efficacy is described as demonstrated on proof-of-principle and real data. GitHub paths in the PDF differ slightly from the catalog abstract (em-thickness-estimation vs z-spacing). Catalog stages include graph_analysis, which is not the paper’s topic.

plain_language_summary: When brain tissue is sliced for the electron microscope, slices are not perfectly even or always in order, which warps the 3D picture. This paper infers the true spacing and order from the images themselves and offers free software to correct it.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomics needs chemical-synapse locations in highly anisotropic serial TEM, where voxels are much coarser in z than in x–y. A detector that trains from sparse labels and does not require a prior cell segmentation would scale more cheaply.
ocar.challenge: Pixel classifiers still miss synapses; object-level false positives include myelinated membranes. Fully annotated subvolumes are expensive.
ocar.action: Kreshuk, Hamprecht, Bock and colleagues, in PLOS ONE (2014), classify pixels with 3D features, segment with an Ising MRF, then classify objects, training on sparse ilastik labels. They test on 20 serial 7197×7351-pixel sections of mouse visual cortex at 4.5×4.5×45 nm with 238 gold-standard synapses from three annotators plus an expert.
ocar.resolution: They report 12% false negatives and 7% false positives, better than a then-current method that required prior cell segmentation. Software and annotations are released via ilastik/vigra.
ocar.future_work: They suggest seeking remaining missed synapses for training and adding myelinated-membrane segmentation to cut object-level false positives.

summaries.beginner: In stacked electron-microscope photos, connections look like tiny dark patches that are easy to miss. This program learns from a few human clicks to find those patches automatically in mouse visual cortex.
summaries.intermediate: In PLOS ONE (2014), Kreshuk et al. detect chemical synapses in anisotropic ssTEM without a prior neuron segmentation. On a 238-synapse mouse visual-cortex stack (4.5×4.5×45 nm; 20 sections), they report 12% false negatives and 7% false positives after two-stage learning in ilastik. Training uses sparse labels rather than a fully painted volume.
summaries.advanced: Error rates are on this 20-section test set, not whole-cortex. “Better than state-of-the-art” is versus a method that needed cell segmentation. Catalog methods include ilastik interactive ML and serial-section EM; organism is mouse. Outlook still flags missed synapses and myelin-related false positives.

plain_language_summary: In stacked electron-microscope photos, connections look like tiny dark patches that are easy to miss. This program learns from a few human clicks to find those patches automatically in mouse visual cortex.

ocar.opportunity: Every nervous system is neuromodulated. Because modulators change intrinsic firing and effective synaptic strength, they can reconfigure circuits and massively change output even when anatomy is fixed.
ocar.challenge: New anatomical, genetic, and optical tools risk reinventing modulation lessons from small circuits. Linear structure–function stories fail when the same connectome supports many functional circuits.
ocar.action: Marder, in Neuron (2012), reviews how neuromodulators are delivered (local hormones, cotransmitters, circulation) and how they transform circuit dynamics, drawing on classical small-circuit work and urging that those lessons inform large-brain mapping.
ocar.resolution: The anatomical connectome is framed as a minimal structure; the neuromodulatory environment constructs the functional circuits that generate behavior. Multiple receptors and long pharmacological history are used to argue that modulation is not an optional add-on.
ocar.future_work: She asks circuit-mapping programs to treat modulation and degenerate dynamics as first-class constraints rather than afterthoughts.

summaries.beginner: A static wiring diagram is only a starting point: chemical modulators can retune cells and connections so the same map produces different rhythms. This review explains that idea with lessons from small circuits.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuron (2012), Eve Marder reviews neuromodulation of circuits, arguing that modulators delivered as hormones, cotransmitters, or circulating factors reconfigure effective connectivity. The connectome is a necessary skeleton; functional circuits depend on the modulatory environment. The piece is explicitly aimed at researchers newly mapping large brains with modern tools.
summaries.advanced: This is a review/perspective without new reconstructions. Catalog has empty organism/method tags. Claims are conceptual; no numeric circuit statistics. Stomatogastric and related small-circuit examples are the evidential core.

plain_language_summary: A static wiring diagram is only a starting point: chemical modulators can retune cells and connections so the same map produces different rhythms. This review explains that idea with lessons from small circuits.

ocar.opportunity: A domain-scale retinal connectome with molecular labels could both validate known pathways and reveal extra motifs that geometry-only imaging would miss. The inner plexiform layer is a compact, layered target.
ocar.challenge: Adjacency without contact is common in retina, so light microscopy or low-resolution EM cannot safely infer synapses from proximity. Manual TEM of large columns was previously impractical.
ocar.action: Anderson, Marc and colleagues, in Molecular Vision (2011), assemble RC1: a 16.5-terabyte rabbit retinal column 0.25 mm in diameter at about 2 nm resolution, spanning inner nuclear, inner plexiform, and ganglion cell layers, with markers for GABA, glutamate, glycine, taurine, glutamine, and an activity marker, annotated in Viking.
ocar.resolution: They recover known connections and report new organization: at least 17 AII signaling modes including photopic bipolar and amacrine inputs; bipolar axons as an integration compartment with axonal veto synapses; intercalated glycine–GABA chains and long starburst-associated chains supporting ON–OFF crossover; molecular/excitation clusters of bipolar types. They conclude that only direct visualization of synapses and gap junctions suffices.
ocar.future_work: Deeper RC1 analysis is offered for more complete network descriptions of specific pathways.

summaries.beginner: Researchers photographed a column of rabbit retina in enormous detail and labeled which cells use which chemicals. The map confirms textbook connections but shows the famous AII pathway is far more mixed than a simple night-vision circuit.
summaries.intermediate: In Molecular Vision (2011), Anderson et al. present retinal connectome RC1 (rabbit; ≈2 nm; 16.5 TB; 0.25 mm column) with computational mosaicking/registration and multiuser Viking annotation. Key findings include ≥17 AII signaling modes, bipolar axonal synapses and vetoes, glycinergic–GABAergic chains, and a warning that adjacency is not connectivity. Conventional TEM connectomics is argued to be practical for network discovery.
summaries.advanced: This is rabbit retina, not mouse, despite the catalog organism tag DS09/DS10 mouse retina. “No less than 17” signaling modes is a lower bound from exploration, not an exhaustive census. RC1 is a column, not a whole retina. Gap junctions are invoked as necessary to visualize, not fully quantified here.

plain_language_summary: Researchers photographed a column of rabbit retina in enormous detail and labeled which cells use which chemicals. The map confirms textbook connections but shows the famous AII pathway is far more mixed than a simple night-vision circuit.

ocar.opportunity: Tiled ssTEM can cover large brains at synaptic resolution, but only after mosaics are registered across distortions, missing sections, and appearance change between sections. An automatic, globally consistent, as-rigid-as-possible method would preserve axon continuity and synapse geometry.
ocar.challenge: Stage metadata cannot stitch tiles seamlessly. Adjacent sections are arbitrarily rotated; staining, beam damage, and mechanical warp break correlation-only pipelines that propagate pairwise translations.
ocar.action: Saalfeld, Cardona, Hartenstein, and Tomancak, in Bioinformatics (2010), match SIFT landmarks within and across sections and globally optimize tile poses by least-squares displacement, implemented in TrakEM2/Fiji. They test on synthetic TEM-like data and register 6885 images of a first-instar Drosophila larval brain.
ocar.resolution: They report a fully automatic non-rigid but as-rigid-as-possible reconstruction of that larval-brain ssTEM dataset. They argue global TEM-level brains will enable registering light-microscopy lineage data onto synaptic volumes.
ocar.future_work: They note the difficulty of assessing geometric fidelity without ground truth on real brains, and they point to CATMAID-style analysis as the downstream use.

summaries.beginner: Huge electron-microscope montages of a young fruit-fly brain are warped and shuffled by cutting and staining. This method finds matching landmarks and gently aligns thousands of tiles so cells stay continuous through depth.
summaries.intermediate: In Bioinformatics (2010), Saalfeld et al. register large ssTEM mosaics with SIFT correspondences and a global least-squares pose, aiming to stay as rigid as possible. They demonstrate the method on 6885 images of the first-instar Drosophila larval brain in TrakEM2 (Fiji). Distortion sources include sectioning, staining, and imaging.
summaries.advanced: Precision is evaluated on an artificial TEM-like set; real-brain geometric error versus ground truth is not fully knowable. The 6885-image stack is first-instar larva, matching catalog DS03. This is alignment, not a completed synapse-level connectome.

plain_language_summary: Huge electron-microscope montages of a young fruit-fly brain are warped and shuffled by cutting and staining. This method finds matching landmarks and gently aligns thousands of tiles so cells stay continuous through depth.

ocar.opportunity: Synapses sit at contacts whose geometry comes from neural shapes, so connectomics reduces in large part to image segmentation. Machines that learn to segment from example “true” partitions could replace most manual tracing.
ocar.challenge: Segmentation had been hard to score and hard to optimize. Computers still erred more than humans on general images; connectomes beyond C. elegans were thought to require prohibitive labor.
ocar.action: Jain, Seung, and Turaga, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2010), review metrics that quantify disagreement with human segmentations and machine-learning methods that search for algorithms minimizing those metrics.
ocar.resolution: They report that these advances reduced computer errors dramatically, to the point that correcting remaining errors should be faster than fully manual segmentation, with further labor reductions expected and required for connectomes more complex than C. elegans.
ocar.future_work: Continued reduction of human proofreading is presented as the crucial remaining technology gap.

summaries.beginner: Listing every connection in a brain means coloring in every cell in a huge picture, which people do slowly. This review explains how computers that learn from corrected examples were starting to make that coloring accurate enough to edit rather than draw from scratch.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2010), Jain, Seung, and Turaga argue that connectomics is a segmentation problem and that new disagreement metrics plus learning-to-segment methods had sharply cut errors. They claim human correction of residual errors should already beat fully manual tracing, and that still less labor is needed to exceed the C. elegans connectome in complexity.
summaries.advanced: This is a 2010 review, not a benchmark paper; “dramatically reduced” is qualitative. Catalog organism/dataset (C. elegans / DS01) reflect the complexity bar, not an analysis of White et al. in this article. Later flood-filling and affinity methods postdate this snapshot.

plain_language_summary: Listing every connection in a brain means coloring in every cell in a huge picture, which people do slowly. This review explains how computers that learn from corrected examples were starting to make that coloring accurate enough to edit rather than draw from scratch.

ocar.opportunity: Interpreting human cognition and neuroimaging needs a connection matrix of the human brain—the connectome—as a time-invariant neuroinformatics foundation, analogous to collations already begun in other mammals.
ocar.challenge: No human connection matrix existed, nor a coordinated effort to collect one. Extrapolating macaque anatomy is problematic. Scale, individual variability, and development complicate any first draft.
ocar.action: Sporns, Tononi, and Kötter, in PLOS Computational Biology (2005), name the human connectome, propose a research strategy and scale for a first draft, and discuss neuroinformatics, experimental routes, limitations, and impact on computational and cognitive neuroscience.
ocar.resolution: They argue the dataset would explain how functional states emerge from structure and how function changes when structure is disrupted, emphasizing cortical principles of segregation and integration. The paper launches the term and the program rather than delivering a matrix.
ocar.future_work: They explicitly leave open how to handle variability and development and how to choose the first-draft scale.

summaries.beginner: To understand the human brain as a network, scientists needed a name and a plan for its full connection list. This article coined “connectome” and argued such a map should be built, even though none existed yet.
summaries.intermediate: In PLOS Computational Biology (2005), Sporns, Tononi, and Kötter propose assembling a human connectome: a structural connection matrix as a shared, time-invariant resource. They contrast existing mammalian collations with the absence of a human matrix, critique macaque extrapolation, and outline strategy, scale, variability, and expected impact on interpreting neuroimaging.
summaries.advanced: This is a manifesto, not an EM or MRI dataset. “Connectome” here is large-scale anatomical connectivity, not synapse-resolved reconstruction. Catalog stage is infrastructure, which matches. No numeric human matrix is produced.

plain_language_summary: To understand the human brain as a network, scientists needed a name and a plan for its full connection list. This article coined “connectome” and argued such a map should be built, even though none existed yet.

ocar.opportunity: Aimed grooming shows that touch location is transformed into location-appropriate movement. A complete map of bristle mechanosensory neuron (BMN) partners in an adult fly brain could reveal how somatotopy is implemented in central circuits.
ocar.challenge: How BMNs interface with brain circuits—feedforward excitation/inhibition, gain control, and developmental lineage—was unclear even after peripheral somatotopy and grooming sequences were described.
ocar.action: Calle-Schuler, Santana-Cruz, Hampel, and Seeds, in eLife (2026; research advance), reconstruct nearly all BMN pre- and postsynaptic partners in the FAFB full-adult-fly-brain serial-section EM volume, analyzing second-order partners with at least 5 synapses.
ocar.resolution: Postsynaptic partners dominate and are mixed excitatory and inhibitory. Excitatory cholinergic hemilineage 23b elicits aimed head grooming and connects differentially to BMNs from distinct head locations, a lineage-based parallel somatotopic architecture. Presynaptic partners supply extensive GABAergic-predicted BMN inhibition consistent with gain control of grooming sequences. Early processing is concentrated in the gnathal ganglion/SEZ.
ocar.future_work: The eLife assessment notes that the behavioral link still rests on prior functional work; VNC neurites of partners are not in FAFB. The map is offered as a resource for future physiology.

summaries.beginner: Flies scratch the part of the head that was touched, so the brain must keep a map of where each bristle sits. This study lists almost all the central partners of those touch cells and finds a developmentally related group that preserves location.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2026), Calle-Schuler et al. map a second-order BMN connectome in FAFB for Drosophila head bristles. They report mixed excitatory/inhibitory postsynaptic partners, somatotopic differential wiring of cholinergic hemilineage 23b, and predominant predicted-GABAergic presynaptic inhibition. Organization is ventral (GNG/SEZ) rather than directly onto dorsal higher-order neuropils.
summaries.advanced: “Nearly all” BMN partners is the authors’ claim for reconstructed head BMNs, filtered at ≥5 synapses. Transmitter labels are predictions. Behavior is tied to prior activation studies (Eichler et al., 2024), not new closed-loop physiology here. Catalog dataset DS04 FAFB matches. FAFB lacks the VNC.

plain_language_summary: Flies scratch the part of the head that was touched, so the brain must keep a map of where each bristle sits. This study lists almost all the central partners of those touch cells and finds a developmentally related group that preserves location.

ocar.opportunity: EM connectomes can score whether synapses land on spines, shafts, or somas across millions of contacts, revealing cell-type targeting rules. Doing that from neuron meshes, without reprocessing images, would be cheap enough for whole volumes.
ocar.challenge: Classifying fine postsynaptic structures at volume scale has been computationally heavy. Exceptions to the textbook excitatory-onto-spine rule were hard to census.
ocar.action: Pedigo, Collman and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2026), compute local mesh-geometry features, train a simple classifier on MICrONS mouse visual cortex, and deploy over hundreds of thousands of neurons at a few hundred dollars of cloud cost.
ocar.resolution: They report weighted F1 0.961 for soma/shaft/spine classification and map postsynaptic structures at over 207.3 million MICrONS synapses. Excitatory axons mostly hit excitatory spines, but layer 5 near-projecting and layer 6 corticothalamic cells often hit excitatory shafts. Multi-synaptic spines vary in frequency even within a type. The same model scores weighted F1 0.949 on H01 human cortex without retraining.
ocar.future_work: They release predictions and pipeline code and argue mesh features are a general morphology primitive for future volumes.

summaries.beginner: Whether a contact lands on a spine or a smooth branch changes what it might do, but counting millions of those landings by hand is impossible. This preprint reads the 3D surface of each cell cheaply and labels those targets across a mouse cortical volume, then checks a human volume.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2026), Pedigo et al. classify MICrONS synapses as soma, shaft, or spine from mesh geometry (weighted F1 0.961) across >207.3 million synapses, then transfer to H01 (weighted F1 0.949, no retraining). They highlight expected spine targeting plus shaft-preferring exceptions in L5-NP and L6-CT cells, and variable multi-synapse spines.
summaries.advanced: F1 scores are weighted class averages on the authors’ labels, not proof of biological ground truth for every synapse. Cloud cost is “a few hundred dollars,” not a formal benchmark. Catalog lists mouse and human / DS13 and DS14, which matches. This is a preprint.

plain_language_summary: Whether a contact lands on a spine or a smooth branch changes what it might do, but counting millions of those landings by hand is impossible. This preprint reads the 3D surface of each cell cheaply and labels those targets across a mouse cortical volume, then checks a human volume.

ocar.opportunity: Combining high-resolution EM with light microscopy could link synaptic wiring to molecular identity and activity from nanoscale to mesoscale, including complete fly connectomes and dynamic profiles in mouse and zebrafish.
ocar.challenge: Core methods, data fusion, terabyte-to-petabyte management, spatiotemporal resolution, ethics, and clinical translation remain scattered across the literature.
ocar.action: Ahmed, Tang and colleagues review, in New Medicine (2026), imaging, tissue preparation, computational reconstruction, and multimodal fusion, with emphasis on correlating anatomy and physiology and on synaptic changes in autism spectrum disorder and Alzheimer’s disease.
ocar.resolution: The review surveys the methodological stack and translational hopes rather than presenting a new volume. It treats complete Drosophila connectomes and mammalian activity mapping as recent breakthroughs and flags dataset scale and ethics as open challenges.
ocar.future_work: Improvements in resolution, fusion, and responsible handling of large datasets are presented as continuing needs.

summaries.beginner: Brain maps now mix ultra-detailed electron-microscope wiring with larger-scale light-microscope pictures of cells and activity. This review walks through how those pictures are made, combined, and sometimes aimed at disease.
summaries.intermediate: In New Medicine (2026), Ahmed et al. review EM plus light-microscopy connectomics: preparation, imaging, reconstruction, and data fusion. They cite complete Drosophila connectomes and activity profiles in mice and zebrafish, discuss terabyte-to-petabyte logistics, and consider synaptic mapping in ASD and AD.
summaries.advanced: This is a short review in a clinical-oriented venue, not primary data. Catalog organism fly and dataset zebrafish capture examples, not a single analyzed volume. Disease sections are translational discussion, not new patient reconstructions. Ethical claims are high-level.

plain_language_summary: Brain maps now mix ultra-detailed electron-microscope wiring with larger-scale light-microscope pictures of cells and activity. This review walks through how those pictures are made, combined, and sometimes aimed at disease.

ocar.opportunity: The primate fovea packs more than 50 neuron types into a miniaturized circuit for high-resolution vision, making it a plausible first human CNS connectome. A proofreadable draft of every cell and synapse in a foveal sample would show which pathways dominate human central vision.
ocar.challenge: Synaptic wiring of diverse foveal types had been difficult to complete. How foveal diversity and connectivity differ from peripheral retina and from mouse remained open.
ocar.action: Kim, Dacey and colleagues, in PNAS (2026), use deep learning to segment cells and synapses in human fovea, classify about 3,000 cells into 51 neuronal types and three glial types, and release a working-draft connectome.
ocar.resolution: Midget and small-bistratified circuits are conserved with nonhuman primates, but they report reduced type diversity versus periphery: only 13 retinal ganglion cell types here versus about 20 in peripheral retina and 40+ in mouse. H1 horizontal cells dominate (96% of horizontal cells at this location; 26:1 versus H2) and receive unexpected S-cone input. About 92% of one cone’s output targets five dominant pathways. Midget ganglion cells are ~90% of ganglion cells in the sample.
ocar.future_work: Seventy cells remain unidentified (often truncated at the volume edge). The resource is described as freely available for further proofreading and for relating structure to human color vision.

summaries.beginner: When we look straight at something, a tiny patch of retina called the fovea does the work with tightly packed cell types. This team used computer vision to draft a wiring diagram of a piece of human fovea and found fewer output cell types than in mouse retina, dominated by high-precision pathways.
summaries.intermediate: In PNAS (2026), Kim et al. present a working-draft human foveal EM connectome: ~3,000 cells classified into 51 neuronal and 3 glial types. They emphasize reduced ganglion-cell diversity (13 types), H1 dominance with unexpected S-cone input, conservation of midget and small-bistratified motifs, and five pathways taking ~92% of sampled cone output. Data are intended as a public, proofreadable resource.
summaries.advanced: This is human fovea, not mouse, despite catalog organism/dataset tags pointing at mouse retina. “Working-draft” and remaining 70 unidentified cells are explicit. Densities are for this HFseg1 sample, not the entire fovea. Transcriptomic comparisons (e.g., midget 86% vs 90% here) are cited as similar trends, not identical counts.

plain_language_summary: When we look straight at something, a tiny patch of retina called the fovea does the work with tightly packed cell types. This team used computer vision to draft a wiring diagram of a piece of human fovea and found fewer output cell types than in mouse retina, dominated by high-precision pathways.

ocar.opportunity: Walking rhythms are thought to come from central pattern generators, but no animal had a identified cellular CPG for walking. Complete fly ventral-nerve-cord connectomes make it possible to simulate which identified neurons can oscillate motor output without rhythmic input.
ocar.challenge: CPG mechanisms elsewhere mix intrinsic bursting and network oscillators; the cells and synapses for fly walking were unknown. Many descending neurons could in principle drive legs.
ocar.action: Pugliese, Tuthill, Brunton and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2026), run dynamic simulations of Drosophila VNC connectomes, computationally activate descending neurons, and prune to a minimal rhythm-generating circuit, then test a predicted second descending pathway with optogenetics in behaving flies.
ocar.resolution: DNg100, a known walking command neuron, is the top simulated driver of rhythmic leg motor activity. A three-neuron motif (one inhibitory and two excitatory interneurons) is necessary and sufficient for motor rhythms in all six legs and in four connectome datasets. Simulations predicted DNb08 as another rhythmic driver, confirmed optogenetically.
ocar.future_work: They present this as a putative CPG for walking and other rhythmic leg movements; how it combines with proprioception and gait in intact behavior remains to be fully mapped.

summaries.beginner: Animals can walk with rhythmic muscle patterns even without timed sensory input, but the exact cells that make that rhythm were unknown. Fly nerve-cord simulations pick out a tiny three-cell circuit, and experiments confirm a second command path that also makes the legs tick.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2026), Pugliese et al. simulate Drosophila VNC connectomes and find DNg100 as the leading descending driver of rhythmic motor output. Network pruning isolates a three-interneuron CPG necessary and sufficient across six legs and four connectomes; DNb08 is a predicted second pathway confirmed with optogenetics. Catalog dataset is DS07 VNC (FANC/MANC).
summaries.advanced: “Necessary and sufficient” is within the simulations and isolation experiments as stated, not a claim that no other neurons contribute in the intact fly. Confirmation of DNb08 is optogenetic in behaving animals; DNg100 was already a known walking command neuron. This is a preprint. Four connectome datasets are asserted but not named in the selected front matter.

plain_language_summary: Animals can walk with rhythmic muscle patterns even without timed sensory input, but the exact cells that make that rhythm were unknown. Fly nerve-cord simulations pick out a tiny three-cell circuit, and experiments confirm a second command path that also makes the legs tick.

ocar.opportunity: Retinal cell types and large dendritic arbors need a wide EM field of view. A volume approaching 1 mm² with matched two-photon responses would let rare types and function–morphology links be resolved together.
ocar.challenge: Prior retinal EM volumes were too small for rare types and wide arbors. Automated reconstructions still need human proofreading and scalable cell typing.
ocar.action: Ströh, Euler, Seung, Berens and the Eyewire II consortium, on bioRxiv (2026), release an adult mouse retina EM dataset covering nearly 1 mm²—described as roughly 10–100 times larger than previous retinal EM volumes—with crowd proofreading, ribbon-synapse detection, and pre-EM two-photon calcium imaging including natural movies.
ocar.resolution: Proofreading so far yields more than 8,000 bipolar, 13,000 amacrine, and 4,000 retinal ganglion cells. A human-in-the-loop deep-learning typer recovers all 15 known bipolar types as regular mosaics. More than 30 laboratories are contributing. Automated conventional-synapse detection is still in progress.
ocar.future_work: The resource is aimed at a complete mammalian retinal cell-type catalog and wiring diagram, with open tools (skeliner, MorphoTyper, Neuroglancer, and others).

summaries.beginner: A mouse retina was photographed over a much larger patch than before, after some cells’ visual responses were recorded. Volunteers and labs are correcting the computer’s cell tracings so rare types and big dendritic trees can be named.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2026), the Eyewire II consortium presents nearly 1 mm² of adult mouse retina EM with prior two-photon imaging. Human proofreading of automated reconstructions has yielded >8,000 bipolar, >13,000 amacrine, and >4,000 ganglion cells; bipolar morphology recovers all 15 known types as mosaics. Ribbon synapses are fully detected; conventional synapses are not yet. Catalog methods include EyeWire crowd proofreading.
summaries.advanced: Cell counts are “so far,” not a finished census. The 10–100× size comparison is the authors’ versus prior retinal EM volumes. This is a preprint resource. Catalog dataset DS09/DS10 mouse retina matches. Completeness of rare RGC types is still limited by ongoing proofreading.

plain_language_summary: A mouse retina was photographed over a much larger patch than before, after some cells’ visual responses were recorded. Volunteers and labs are correcting the computer’s cell tracings so rare types and big dendritic trees can be named.

ocar.opportunity: Multiple Drosophila brain and ventral-nerve-cord connectomes now exist, so comparing sexes requires cell typing at scale. Aligning graphs by topology alone could assign types without exhaustive manual curation.
ocar.challenge: Standard cell typing is curation-heavy. Connectomes differ in size; naive alignment can flip left–right; strict one-to-one matching cannot express many-to-one dimorphism.
ocar.action: Matsliah, Salmon, Seung, Murthy and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2026), align connectomes with ACDC using topology only, then build a connectivity-similarity (ConSim) score from weighted Jaccard features, using two complete male VNCs as references for the female VNC.
ocar.resolution: They assign types to about 13,000 intrinsic female VNC neurons and automatically flag sex-specific and sexually dimorphic types, including circuits for male song and female oviposition and their cross-sex counterparts. They argue network topology alone can support large-scale comparative connectomics.
ocar.future_work: They call for scaling alignment across individuals, stages, and species and for integrating non-topological identity cues.

summaries.beginner: Male and female flies control different body actions through the nerve cord, but naming matching cells by hand is slow. This preprint lines up whole wiring diagrams using only who-connects-to-whom and then lists which cell types differ by sex.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2026), Matsliah et al. automatically align Drosophila VNC connectomes from network topology, typing ~13,000 intrinsic female neurons against two male references. They census sex-specific and dimorphic types and compare song versus oviposition circuits across sexes. Methods add padding nodes and auxiliary L/R nodes to ACDC, then ConSim from synchronized synapse-count feature vectors.
summaries.advanced: Type assignment quality depends on alignment confidence and male reference typing. Hemisphere flips are a known degeneracy, constrained here with auxiliary nodes. Catalog dataset DS07 VNC (FANC/MANC) is the setting; BANC-FlyWire is in the author list. This is a preprint.

plain_language_summary: Male and female flies control different body actions through the nerve cord, but naming matching cells by hand is slow. This preprint lines up whole wiring diagrams using only who-connects-to-whom and then lists which cell types differ by sex.

ocar.opportunity: Mitochondria set energy and calcium handling in neurons, but connectomes rarely treat their shape and position as circuit variables. Measuring them across many identified cells could reveal rules that link organelles to synapses and cell types.
ocar.challenge: It was unknown whether mitochondrial morphology is type-specific enough to fingerprint neurons, how precisely mitochondria sit relative to synapses, and whether positioning rules generalize from fly to mouse cortex.
ocar.action: Sager, Schreiber, Clark and colleagues, in Science (catalog year 2025; published 2026), analyze mitochondrial morphology and placement in an EM Drosophila connectome (visual projection neurons in the catalog abstract; hundreds of thousands of mitochondria across thousands of neurons in the article abstract) and compare with a mouse visual-cortex connectome.
ocar.resolution: Shape and size differ systematically by cell and transmitter type. Mitochondria sit with 2–3 μm precision relative to synaptic and structural features, with axon/dendrite and cell-type differences that correlate with visual responses and connectivity. In olfactory learning circuits they enrich at presynapses onto particular targets via axonal subcompartments. Mouse cortex confirms type-specific morphology with partly divergent positioning rules.
ocar.future_work: They propose mitochondria as circuit-embedded organelles whose snapshot in EM volumes may also reflect recent activity, inviting functional tests of the positioning rules.

summaries.beginner: Energy-producing mitochondria are not sprinkled at random inside brain cells. Across a fly wiring diagram they have characteristic shapes per cell type and sit a few microns from particular synapses, with some of the same ideas holding in mouse cortex.
summaries.intermediate: In Science (2025 catalog year), Sager et al. quantify mitochondrial morphology and 2–3 μm-scale positioning in a Drosophila EM connectome and test related rules in mouse visual cortex. Morphology fingerprints cell and neurotransmitter types; placement differs by compartment and type and tracks activity and postsynaptic identity, including enrichment in mushroom-body axonal subcompartments. Catalog tags include fly and DS13 MICrONS (the mouse comparison volume).
summaries.advanced: The catalog abstract’s “>100,000 mitochondria in over 1,000 visual projection neurons” and the article abstract’s “hundreds of thousands… thousands of neurons” describe nested scopes; do not collapse them. Positioning “precision of 2–3 μm” is the stated scale, not a synapse-by-synapse distance table. Mouse rules are “partially divergent.” Organelle annotations inherit EM segmentation error.
